pairs.en: On the same day, the twelfth of the month, we remember the holy martyrs PHOTIOS and ANIKETOS.
*A fire unconquerable blazes with Photios,* *whom the house of Light brings forth as unconquered.* *On the twelfth, fire slew Photios and Aniketos.*
These saints lived in the time of the emperor Diocletian, in the year 288; Photios was the nephew of Saint Aniketos.

Now Diocletian made a public speech against the Christians in Nicomedia, with the Senate itself present. That most ungodly man had many kinds of torture instruments set out in the middle, and threatened that he would wipe out, by every means, all those who call on the name of Christ, and drive them from the very ends of the earth. When, I say, this wretched tyrant blasphemed against the Godhead and glory of the only-begotten Son of God, then the martyr of Christ Aniketos, who was present, did not fear the tyrant's threats. He freely confessed himself a Christian, and he rebuked and pilloried the error of the idols, adding this too: that those who worship idols are deaf and without feeling. For these words the idol-worshippers beat the saint so severely that the blows of the rods left his body a mass of wounds and gashes, through which his bones showed. Then the emperor let loose a lion against him. The saint was afraid when he saw it, because it was not only huge in body, not only charging with fury and madness, but on top of that it roared a fearful and terrifying roar. Yet when it came near the saint, it grew gentler than a sheep; and as if sharing the martyr's suffering, it kept wiping with its right paw the sweat that fear had poured over his face. Then the saint gave thanks to God; and at the end of the thanksgiving an earthquake came. From the earthquake the idol of Herakles fell down and became as dust; and part of the city of Nicomedia was thrown down as well, crushing many pagans.

So the emperor ordered them to behead the martyr. But the soldier who was to behead the saint was left powerless — his hand was seized, and he could not bring down the sword. So the emperor changed his sentence: he bound the saint to a wheel and laid a fire beneath it. There, while his limbs were being cut by the wheel and burned by the fire, he prayed to God; and as he prayed — O the wonder! — the bonds came loose, the wheel stood still, and the fire went out. Then his nephew Photios too ran to the saint's side, and embracing him, called him father and mother and his own uncle. So he too was bound with his uncle in iron chains, and the two were thrown into prison. Then they were torn, and burned with fire, and stoned by the mob in the theatre. Preserved unharmed through all these torments, the athletes of Christ were hung from wooden posts by their feet and dragged by wild horses; after that they were beaten again, severely, and their wounded limbs were rubbed with salt and vinegar. Then, thrown into prison, they were left there untended for three whole years. When they had been withered by the long hardship of prison, the tyrant heated for three days the bath called the Bath of Antoninus, and shut the saints inside it. But as they prayed, the floor of the bath split open, and a mass of water welled up from below, so that the saints seemed to be not in a fired-up bath but in a cool garden. Finally the ungodly Diocletian took counsel and built a furnace in the shape of a smelting-pot, fixed upon iron pillars. Thrown into this, the saints prayed and gave their souls into the hands of God, and so they received from him the crowns of their contest. They say that from the time the saints were put into the furnace they remained alive for three days; and when their bodies were dragged out of the furnace with iron tools, they were sound and whole — the fire had not harmed even a single hair of their head. Their gathering and feast is kept at their most holy church, in the place called Strategion. (Note that the Greek account of their martyrdom is found in the Great Lavra; it begins: “When Diocletian, the sacrilegious one, was reigning.”)
The venerable PALAMON died in peace.
*Palamon, you give your soul into God's hands,* *showing it proof against the hands of the soul-destroyer.*

This venerable Palamon was the elder, and the wise and experienced teacher, of the great Pachomios; see about him in the full life of Pachomios, found in the Kalokairine (the summer service book), on the fifteenth of May.

sections.heading: The Twelve Martyrs, Soldiers, from Crete

pairs.en: The holy TWELVE martyrs, soldiers by calling, who came from Crete, died by the sword.
*A company of martyrs contends by the sword,* *equal in number to Christ's own chosen disciples.*
(In other copies the last word of the couplet is written “from Crete” instead of “chosen”.)
The venerable KASTOR died in peace.
*The great Kastor, a divine lamp-wick, is quenched —* *the oil of this life burning itself out into light.*
The holy martyrs PAMPHILOS and KAPITON died by the sword.
*Lying on the ground, steeped in gore,* *Pamphilos and Kapiton met the sword.*
The venerable SERGIOS and STEPHANOS died in peace.
*For Sergios and Stephanos, equal in their sweats,* *equal crowns — for so it is fitting.*
Through the prayers of your Saints, Christ our God, have mercy on us.
